## A wider field of view
THE FRONTIER is a public research and learning publication. Its starting point is a simple habit: follow a good question beyond the boundary of one subject.

A conversation about video compression can lead to machine perception. A question about automation can lead to wages, ownership and consumer demand. Neither question belongs to just one discipline.

This is an evergreen opening guide, not a report of today's discoveries. Daily briefings will appear here after research and source checks are complete.

## Read for the mechanism
For each development, ask what problem the researchers were trying to solve, what changed in their approach, and what evidence supports the result. Then ask what the experiment leaves unresolved.

A useful explanation should let you describe the mechanism in your own words. If it only lets you repeat the headline, keep reading.

## Evidence has a shape
A preprint is an invitation to inspect a result, not a certificate that the result is settled. A benchmark measures performance under particular conditions. A policy proposal is different from an enacted rule. An institutional statement is evidence of that institution's position, not independent proof of every claim it makes.

Keep those distinctions beside the claim. The aim is informed curiosity, with uncertainty left visible.

## Start with a real classroom
[MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/) is a place to build foundations in science, engineering and economics. Pick a course that supplies the prerequisites for a question you already care about. Where video lectures are available, work through the exercises alongside them.

[Complexity Explorer at the Santa Fe Institute](https://www.complexityexplorer.org/) offers a route into complex systems. Use it to explore how interactions between parts can produce behaviour that is difficult to infer from the parts alone.

[The Simons Institute video library](https://simons.berkeley.edu/videos) provides research talks and public lectures in theoretical computing. Start with a public lecture; specialist workshop talks may assume substantial mathematics.

These are verified learning libraries, not claims that a particular lecture was released today. Durations vary and are not estimated here.

## A question to keep
When a technology makes production cheaper, what else must change for more people to benefit?

Keep separate notes for the technical possibility, the economic mechanism, the institutional choice and the evidence you would need. Future editions will return to questions like this with specific research, competing explanations and sources you can inspect.
